questions.question: Write 17/5 as a mixed number.
questions.explain: Divide 17 by 5: 5 goes in 3 times with 2 left over, so 17/5 = 3 2/5. The leftover 2 stays over the SAME denominator 5 — don't swap the whole number and numerator, and don't change the denominator.

questions.question: Write the mixed number 4 3/8 as an improper fraction.
questions.explain: Multiply the whole number by the denominator, then add the numerator: 4 × 8 = 32, 32 + 3 = 35, so 4 3/8 = 35/8. The most common slip is stopping at 32/8 (forgetting to add the 3) or just adding 4 + 3 to get 7/8.

questions.question: Which one of these fractions is greater than 1 whole?
questions.explain: A fraction is greater than 1 when the numerator is bigger than the denominator (an improper fraction): 9 > 8, so 9/8 = 1 1/8. Fractions like 5/6 look 'big' because the numbers are close, but 5 < 6 means it is still less than 1.

questions.question: A point on a number line sits exactly halfway between 2 and 3. Which number is at that point?
questions.explain: Halfway between 2 and 3 is 2 1/2, and 2 1/2 = (2 × 2 + 1)/2 = 5/2. Watch out: 3/2 and 5/4 both land between 1 and 2, not between 2 and 3.

questions.question: In math class, a hexagon pattern block is 1 whole and a green triangle is 1/6 of it. Nadia lays out 11 green triangles. How much is that, written as a mixed number?
questions.explain: 11 triangles is 11/6; six of them build 1 hexagon and 5 are left over, so 11/6 = 1 5/6. The leftover pieces are still sixths, so the denominator stays 6 — it does not become 11.

questions.question: After soccer practice, Jayden drank 7/12 L of water and Priya drank 5/8 L. Who drank more?
options: Jayden, because twelfths are bigger pieces than eighths
They drank the same, because both are just over 1/2 L
questions.explain: Use a common denominator: 24. 7/12 = 14/24 and 5/8 = 15/24, so Priya drank more. You cannot compare by numerators alone, and a bigger denominator actually means smaller pieces, not bigger ones.

questions.question: On the seawall, Ana walked 11/4 km on Saturday and 2 5/8 km on Sunday. On which day did she walk farther?
options: Sunday, because a mixed number is always greater than an improper fraction
Sunday, because 11/4 = 2 1/4, which is less than 2 5/8
They walked the same distance both days
Saturday, because 11/4 = 2 6/8, which is more than 2 5/8
questions.explain: Change 11/4 to a mixed number: 11 ÷ 4 = 2 with 3 left over, so 11/4 = 2 3/4 = 2 6/8, which beats 2 5/8. The trap is misreading the remainder (2 1/4) or assuming an improper fraction must be smaller because it has no whole number in front.

questions.question: Diego models a number with fraction circles that are each cut into fourths. He fills 3 whole circles and shades 2 more fourths on a fourth circle. Which improper fraction shows how many fourths he has in all?
questions.explain: Each whole circle is 4 fourths, so 3 wholes = 12 fourths, plus the 2 extra fourths = 14/4. Common slips are counting only the whole circles (12/4), adding 3 + 2 to get 5/4, or writing the digits side by side as 32/4.

questions.question: Three jugs are set out at a class picnic: jug A holds 3 L, jug B holds 13/4 L, and jug C holds 3 1/8 L. Which list puts them in order from least to greatest?
questions.explain: First change 13/4 to 3 1/4, then use eighths: 3 = 3 0/8, 3 1/8, and 3 1/4 = 3 2/8, giving 3 L, 3 1/8 L, 13/4 L. The usual mistake is thinking 1/8 > 1/4 because 8 > 4 — with the same numerator, more pieces in the whole means each piece is smaller.

questions.question: For a birchbark biting demonstration, an Elder folds and bites one design out of each 1/4 sheet of birchbark. She plans 15 designs, and the bark comes only in whole sheets. How many whole sheets does she need to bring?
questions.explain: 15 quarter-sheets is 15/4 = 3 3/4 sheets, but bark comes in whole sheets, so 3 sheets leaves her 3 designs short and she must bring 4. The trap is stopping at the mixed number 3 3/4 instead of asking what a whole sheet means in the story.

questions.question: Using fraction strips, Leo shades 9/6 of a strip and Mia shades 5/3 of a strip. Who shaded more?
options: Leo, because his model uses more shaded pieces
They shaded the same amount, because both are between 1 and 2
questions.explain: Rename to a common denominator: 5/3 = 10/6, and 10/6 > 9/6, so Mia shaded more. Bigger-looking numbers do not mean a bigger fraction — 9/6 is made of smaller sixths, so more pieces can still be less.

questions.question: Ravi needs 5 3/4 m of ribbon for a school banner. The ribbon is sold as pre-cut quarter-metre (1/4 m) pieces. How many pieces must he buy to have exactly that much?
questions.explain: Change 5 3/4 into fourths: 5 × 4 = 20, plus 3 more fourths = 23/4, so he needs 23 pieces. The most common error is forgetting to add the 3 (getting 20) or rounding up to 6 whole metres (getting 24).
